examples.ko: 이번 시험을 망치면 내 성적은 끝장나요.
examples.en: If I mess up this exam, my grades are done for.
The relationship between the two ended that very day.

examples.ko: 이대로 가면 우리 회사가 끝장날지도 몰라요.
examples.en: If we keep going like this, our company might be finished.

examples.ko: 저 가게는 장사가 안 돼서 곧 끝장날 것 같아요.
examples.en: That shop isn't doing well and seems about to go under.

examples.ko: 다 끝장났다고 생각했는데 다시 기회가 왔어요.
examples.en: I thought it was all over, but another chance came.

examples.ko: 그 소문이 퍼지면 그 사람 인생은 끝장날 수도 있어요.
examples.en: If that rumor spreads, that person's life could be ruined.

explain: '끝나다'보다 훨씬 강하게, 더 이상 가망이 없이 망한다는 부정적인 느낌이에요. 관계, 사업, 계획이 완전히 무너질 때 구어로 많이 써요. 일상적인 일이 단순히 끝나는 것에는 '끝나다'를 써야 해요.
explain_en: It is much stronger than '끝나다' and carries a negative sense of something being ruined beyond hope. In speech it is used when a relationship, business, or plan completely collapses. For things that simply finish, use '끝나다'.

en: be forced out; be driven out; be expelled

examples.ko: 그는 집세를 못 내서 집에서 내쫓겼어요.
examples.en: He couldn't pay the rent and was kicked out of his house.
The stray cat keeps getting chased away from in front of the shop.
I'm anxious that I might be pushed out of the company.
I broke a promise and ended up being kicked out of the group.
I ended up in a situation of being thrown out by the owner.
I was suddenly thrown out and had nowhere to go.

explain: '내쫓다'(몰아내다)의 피동이에요. '집에서 내쫓기다'처럼 장소는 '-에서', 내쫓은 사람은 '-에게'로 말해요. '쫓겨나다'도 비슷한 뜻으로 써요.
explain_en: It is the passive of '내쫓다' (to drive out). The place takes '-에서' and the person who drove you out takes '-에게', as in '집에서 내쫓기다'. '쫓겨나다' is used with a similar meaning.

examples.en: I prepare for the chance of rain.
I study every day to prepare for the exam.
There was a drill to prepare for earthquakes.
I bought clothes in preparation for winter.
To prepare for later, you have to save.
I'll be ready for the worst case.

explain: '대비하다'는 일어날지 모르는 일을 미리 준비할 때 써요. '준비하다'는 해야 할 일을 갖추는 것이고, '대비하다'는 나쁜 일이나 변화에 맞서 갖추는 것이에요. 보통 '~에 대비하다'로 써요.
explain_en: 대비하다 is used when you prepare in advance for something that might happen. 준비하다 is getting ready for something you have to do, while 대비하다 is getting ready against bad events or change. It is usually '~에 대비하다'.

examples.en: The hunter set a trap in the forest.

examples.ko: 작은 새가 덫에 걸려서 날지 못했어요.
examples.en: A small bird got caught in a trap and couldn't fly.
This email might be a scammer's trap.

examples.ko: 덫이 너무 튼튼해서 고양이가 빠져나오지 못했어요.
examples.en: The trap was so sturdy that the cat couldn't get out.

examples.ko: 그 사람의 덫에 빠지지 않게 조심하세요.
examples.en: Be careful not to fall into that person's trap.
Don't sign a contract that feels like a trap.

explain: 동물을 잡는 도구가 덫이고, 쥐를 잡는 것은 '쥐덫'처럼 앞에 대상을 붙여요. '함정'은 구덩이 같은 느낌이 강하고, 덫은 한번 걸리면 빠져나오기 힘든 느낌이에요. '덫을 놓다', '덫에 걸리다'가 대표적이에요.

phrases.nuance_ko: 동물이 아니라 사람이 남의 속임수나 나쁜 상황에 빠질 때도 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: It is also used when a person, not an animal, gets caught in someone's trick or a bad situation.

explain_en: The tool that catches animals is a 덫, and you attach the target in front, as in 쥐덫 (mouse trap). 함정 feels more like a pit, while 덫 feels like something that is hard to escape once caught. Typical uses are 덫을 놓다 and 덫에 걸리다.

examples.en: The road was blocked, so I turned back.

examples.ko: 그는 문 앞에서 갑자기 되돌아서 나갔어요.
examples.en: He suddenly turned around at the door and went out.

examples.ko: 이미 너무 멀리 와서 되돌아설 수는 없어요.
examples.en: We've come too far to turn back.
The moment I was about to turn back, someone called me.
His back as he turned away looked lonely.

examples.ko: 마음을 바꿔 되돌아서면 아직 늦지 않아요.
examples.en: If you change your mind and turn back, it's not too late.

explain: '돌아서다'가 몸의 방향을 바꾸는 것이라면, '되돌아서다'는 왔던 쪽으로 다시 몸을 돌리는 느낌이 있어요. 길을 되돌아갈 때는 '되돌아가다'를 같이 쓰기도 해요.
explain_en: While '돌아서다' means simply turning around, '되돌아서다' feels like turning back toward where you came from. When you actually go back along the road, '되돌아가다' is often used alongside it.

examples.en: I secretly eavesdropped on the people next to me.

examples.ko: 남의 전화를 엿듣는 건 예의가 아니에요.
examples.en: It's rude to eavesdrop on other people's phone calls.
Don't eavesdrop at the door; come in.
My younger sibling was listening in on our talk.
The conversation I overheard at the cafe was so funny.

examples.ko: 누가 엿들을까 봐 작은 목소리로 말했어요.
examples.en: I spoke quietly in case someone was listening in.

explain: 남이 모르게 몰래 듣는다는 느낌이라, 우연히 들린 것은 '듣게 되다'로 말하는 편이 자연스러워요. '듣다'처럼 ㄷ 불규칙이라서 '엿들어요', '엿들었어요', '엿들은'으로 바뀌어요.
explain_en: It carries the feeling of listening secretly, so for something you just happened to hear, '듣게 되다' sounds more natural. Like '듣다' it is a ㄷ-irregular verb, giving '엿들어요', '엿들었어요' and '엿들은'.

examples.en: The house was surrounded by reporters.
The army was encircled by the enemy in the mountains.
The people who were surrounded waited for rescue.

examples.ko: 차에 탄 채 팬들에게 포위돼서 움직일 수 없었어요.
examples.en: Still in the car, I was surrounded by fans and could not move.
The thief gave up once the police surrounded him.
All sides were blocked, and it felt like being surrounded.

explain: 포위되다는 사방이 막혀 빠져나갈 길이 없는 상태를 말해요. 기자·팬·경찰에게 둘러싸이는 장면에 자주 써요. 쓰기는 '~에게 포위되다'예요.
explain_en: 포위되다 is the state of being hemmed in on all sides with no way out, often in scenes of being mobbed by reporters, fans or police. The pattern is '~에게 포위되다'.
